amc12-ahsme-1952-01.title: Rational times $\pi$
amc12-ahsme-1952-01.body:
The area is $\pi r^2$. If $r\ne0$ is rational, $r^2$ is a nonzero rational, and a nonzero rational times the irrational number $\pi$ is irrational.

**Answer: (B) irrational**

amc12-ahsme-1952-01.title: Why the product is irrational
amc12-ahsme-1952-01.body:
If $\pi r^2=q$ were rational, then $\pi=\frac{q}{r^2}$ would be a quotient of rationals, hence rational — but $\pi$ is irrational. So the area is irrational (e.g. $r=1$ gives area $\pi$).

**Answer: (B) irrational**

amc12-ahsme-1952-02.title: Total points
amc12-ahsme-1952-02.body:
The total is $20\cdot80+30\cdot70=1600+2100=3700$ over $50$ students, an average of $74\%$.

**Answer: (B) $74\%$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-02.title: Weighted average
amc12-ahsme-1952-02.body:
The average lies between $70$ and $80$, closer to $70$ in the ratio $20:30$: $70+\frac{20}{50}\cdot10=74$.

**Answer: (B) $74\%$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-04.title: Count the additional pounds
amc12-ahsme-1952-04.body:
After the first pound there are $P-1$ additional pounds at $3$ cents each: $C=10+3(P-1)$.

**Answer: (C) $C=10+3(P-1)$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-04.title: Check values
amc12-ahsme-1952-04.body:
$P=1$ costs $10$ and $P=2$ costs $13$. (C) gives $10$ and $13$ ✓. (A) gives $13$ for $P=1$; (D) $C=9+3P$ gives $12$ for $P=1$; (E) gives $13$ for $P=2$ but $3$ for $P=1$.

**Answer: (C) $C=10+3(P-1)$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-05.title: Midpoint
amc12-ahsme-1952-05.body:
$(3,3)$ is the midpoint of $(6,12)$ and $(0,-6)$, so it certainly lies on the segment joining them.

**Answer: (A) $(3,3)$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-06.title: Quadratic formula
amc12-ahsme-1952-06.body:
The roots are $\frac{7\pm\sqrt{49+36}}{2}=\frac{7\pm\sqrt{85}}{2}$; their difference is $\sqrt{85}$.

**Answer: (E) $\sqrt{85}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-06.title: Vieta
amc12-ahsme-1952-06.body:
$(r-s)^2=(r+s)^2-4rs=49+36=85$, so $r-s=\sqrt{85}$ (taking the larger minus the smaller).

**Answer: (E) $\sqrt{85}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-08.title: List the positions
amc12-ahsme-1952-08.body:
Two equal (distinct) circles can be separate ($4$ common tangents), externally tangent ($3$), or intersecting in two points ($2$). Exactly $1$ common tangent happens only for internally tangent circles, which needs different radii.

**Answer: (A) $1$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-08.title: Why not 1
amc12-ahsme-1952-08.body:
Internal tangency means the distance between centers is $|r_1-r_2|$, which is $0$ for equal circles — they would coincide (infinitely many tangents). So equal circles never have exactly one common tangent.

**Answer: (A) $1$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-09.title: Check
amc12-ahsme-1952-09.body:
Take $a=2$, $b=1$, $c=1$: $m=\frac{2}{1}=2$. (D) gives $\frac{4}{2+2}=1$ ✓. Choices (A) and (B) still contain $b$, so they don't solve for it.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{ma}{m+ca}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-10.title: Pick a distance
amc12-ahsme-1952-10.body:
Say the hill is $20$ miles. Up takes $2$ h, down $1$ h: $40$ miles in $3$ h, i.e. $13\frac13$ mph.

**Answer: (B) $13\frac{1}{3}$ mph**

amc12-ahsme-1952-10.title: Harmonic mean
amc12-ahsme-1952-10.body:
For equal distances, average speed $=\frac{2\cdot10\cdot20}{10+20}=\frac{400}{30}=13\frac13$ mph.

**Answer: (B) $13\frac{1}{3}$ mph**

amc12-ahsme-1952-11.title: Check $f(1)$
amc12-ahsme-1952-11.body:
At $x=1$ the denominator is $0$, so $f(1)$ is undefined — it certainly isn't $0$. The rest are true: $f(0)=\frac2{-1}=-2$, $f(-2)=0$, and solving $y(x-1)=x+2$ gives $x(y-1)=y+2$, i.e. $x=\frac{y+2}{y-1}=f(y)$.

**Answer: (C) $f(1)=0$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-11.title: Self-inverse function
amc12-ahsme-1952-11.body:
$f(f(x))=\frac{\frac{x+2}{x-1}+2}{\frac{x+2}{x-1}-1}=\frac{3x}{3}=x$, so $f$ is its own inverse; that confirms (A) and (E). (B) and (D) are direct substitutions. Only (C) fails, since $f(1)$ is undefined.

**Answer: (C) $f(1)=0$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-12.title: Two equations
amc12-ahsme-1952-12.body:
$\frac{a}{1-r}=6$ and $a(1+r)=\frac92$. Dividing: $(1-r)(1+r)=\frac{9/2}{6}=\frac34$, so $r^2=\frac14$, $r=\pm\frac12$. Then $a=6(1-r)=3$ or $9$.

**Answer: (E) $9$ or $3$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-13.title: Vertex formula
amc12-ahsme-1952-13.body:
The vertex of $ax^2+bx+c$ is at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}=-\frac p2$; since the leading coefficient is positive, this is a minimum.

**Answer: (E) $x=\frac{-p}{2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-14.title: Find the costs
amc12-ahsme-1952-14.body:
House: $0.8\cdot\text{cost}=12000$, cost $15000$. Store: $1.2\cdot\text{cost}=12000$, cost $10000$. Total cost $25000$, total received $24000$: a loss of $\$1000$.

**Answer: (B) loss of $\$1000$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-14.title: Losses and gains
amc12-ahsme-1952-14.body:
The house lost $15000-12000=3000$ and the store gained $12000-10000=2000$. Net: loss of $\$1000$. (The percentages are of different costs, so they don't cancel.)

**Answer: (B) loss of $\$1000$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-15.title: Compare squares
amc12-ahsme-1952-15.body:
The largest angle is opposite the side $9$. Since $6^2+8^2=100>81=9^2$, that angle is less than $90^\circ$, so all angles are acute.

**Answer: (C) the triangle is acute**

amc12-ahsme-1952-15.title: Law of cosines
amc12-ahsme-1952-15.body:
$\cos(\text{largest angle})=\frac{36+64-81}{2\cdot6\cdot8}=\frac{19}{96}>0$, so the largest angle is acute (about $78.6^\circ$). Angles are not proportional to sides, ruling out (B); the smallest angle is about $41.4^\circ$, and $2\cdot41.4\ne78.6$, ruling out (D).

**Answer: (C) the triangle is acute**

amc12-ahsme-1952-16.title: Inverse factor
amc12-ahsme-1952-16.body:
New altitude $=\frac{1}{1.1}=\frac{10}{11}$ of the old one, a decrease of $\frac1{11}=9\frac1{11}\%$.

**Answer: (E) $9\frac{1}{11}\%$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-16.title: Numbers
amc12-ahsme-1952-16.body:
Base $10$, altitude $11$, area $110$. New base $11$ needs altitude $10$: a decrease of $1$ out of $11$, i.e. $9\frac1{11}\%$.

**Answer: (E) $9\frac{1}{11}\%$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-17.title: List price 100
amc12-ahsme-1952-17.body:
Cost $=80$. Marked price $M$, selling price $0.8M$. Profit is $20\%$ of the selling price, so cost $=80\%$ of the selling price: $80=0.8\cdot0.8M=0.64M$, $M=125$.

**Answer: (C) $125$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-17.title: Check
amc12-ahsme-1952-17.body:
List $100$, cost $80$, marked $125$, sold at $100$. Profit $20$, which is $20\%$ of the selling price $100$ ✓.

**Answer: (C) $125$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-19.title: Angle bisector theorem twice
amc12-ahsme-1952-19.body:
Order the points $A,D,E,C$ on $AC$. In triangle $ABE$, $BD$ bisects $\angle ABE$, so $\frac{AD}{DE}=\frac{AB}{BE}$. In triangle $DBC$, $BE$ bisects $\angle DBC$, so $\frac{DE}{EC}=\frac{BD}{BC}$. Multiplying: $\frac{AD}{EC}=\frac{AB\cdot BD}{BE\cdot BC}$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{AD}{EC}=\frac{(AB)(BD)}{(BE)(BC)}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-19.title: Areas
amc12-ahsme-1952-19.body:
Let each third of angle $B$ be $\theta$. Triangles $ABD$ and $EBC$ have the same height from $B$ to $AC$, so $\frac{AD}{EC}=\frac{[ABD]}{[EBC]}=\frac{\frac12AB\cdot BD\sin\theta}{\frac12BE\cdot BC\sin\theta}=\frac{AB\cdot BD}{BE\cdot BC}$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{AD}{EC}=\frac{(AB)(BD)}{(BE)(BC)}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-20.title: Algebra
amc12-ahsme-1952-20.body:
$\frac{x-y}{y}=\frac xy-1=\frac34-1=-\frac14$, so (E) has the wrong sign.

**Answer: (E) $\frac{x-y}{y}=\frac{1}{4}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-21.title: Triangle on each side
amc12-ahsme-1952-21.body:
Each point of the star is the apex of a triangle built on one side of the polygon, formed by extending the two neighboring sides. The base angles of that triangle are exterior angles of the polygon, $\frac{360}{n}$ each. So the point angle is $180-\frac{720}{n}=\frac{(n-4)180}{n}$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{(n-4)180}{n}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-21.title: Check with stars you know
amc12-ahsme-1952-21.body:
For $n=5$ the pentagram has $36^\circ$ points: (B) gives $\frac{180}{5}=36$ ✓, while (A) gives $72$, (C) $108$, (D) $162$. For $n=6$ the six-pointed star has $60^\circ$ points: (B) gives $\frac{2\cdot180}{6}=60$ ✓, while (E) gives $30$. Only (B) survives both checks.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{(n-4)180}{n}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-22.title: Example
amc12-ahsme-1952-22.body:
If $b=2$, then $AB=\sqrt5$, and with $AD=2$, $BD=1$. (B) gives $\sqrt{4-3}=1$ ✓; (E) gives $\sqrt7$.

**Answer: (B) $\sqrt{b^2-3}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-23.title: Zero sum of roots
amc12-ahsme-1952-23.body:
Cross-multiply: $(m+1)(x^2-bx)=(m-1)(ax-c)$, i.e. $(m+1)x^2-[b(m+1)+a(m-1)]x+c(m-1)=0$. Roots $r$ and $-r$ have sum $0$, so the $x$-coefficient vanishes: $b(m+1)+a(m-1)=0$, $m(a+b)=a-b$, $m=\frac{a-b}{a+b}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{a-b}{a+b}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-23.title: Use the ratio
amc12-ahsme-1952-23.body:
Write $k=\frac{m-1}{m+1}$. The equation is $x^2-bx=k(ax-c)$, i.e. $x^2-(b+ka)x+kc=0$. Opposite roots need $b+ka=0$, $k=-\frac ba$. Then $\frac{m-1}{m+1}=-\frac ba$ gives $a(m-1)=-b(m+1)$, $m=\frac{a-b}{a+b}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{a-b}{a+b}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-24.title: Subtract a similar triangle
amc12-ahsme-1952-24.body:
$BC=\sqrt{400-144}=16$, so $[ABC]=\frac12\cdot12\cdot16=96$. Triangle $BDE$ (right angle at $D$) is similar to $BCA$ (right angle at $C$) since they share $\angle B$. With $BD=10$: $\frac{DE}{BD}=\frac{AC}{BC}=\frac{12}{16}$, so $DE=7.5$ and $[BDE]=\frac12\cdot10\cdot7.5=37.5$. Then $[ADEC]=96-37.5=58\frac12$.

**Answer: (B) $58\frac{1}{2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-24.title: Area ratio
amc12-ahsme-1952-24.body:
The similarity ratio of $BDE$ to $BCA$ is $\frac{BD}{BC}=\frac{10}{16}=\frac58$, so $[BDE]=\left(\frac58\right)^2\cdot96=\frac{25}{64}\cdot96=37.5$. The quadrilateral has area $96-37.5=58.5$.

**Answer: (B) $58\frac{1}{2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-25.title: Catch-up equation
amc12-ahsme-1952-25.body:
Work in feet: he runs $24$ ft/s. At time $t\ge30$ the sound has traveled $1080(t-30)$ ft, and he is $24t$ ft away. They meet when $1080(t-30)=24t$, so $1056t=32400$, $t\approx30.68$ s. He has run $8t\approx245$ yd.

**Answer: (D) $245$ yd.**

amc12-ahsme-1952-25.title: Head start
amc12-ahsme-1952-25.body:
At the blast he is $240$ yd $=720$ ft away. The sound gains on him at $1080-24=1056$ ft/s, so it reaches him $\frac{720}{1056}\approx0.68$ s later, during which he runs about $5.5$ yd more: $\approx245$ yd.

**Answer: (D) $245$ yd.**

amc12-ahsme-1952-26.title: Factor
amc12-ahsme-1952-26.body:
$r^3+\frac1{r^3}=\left(r+\frac1r\right)\left(r^2-1+\frac1{r^2}\right)$, and $r^2+\frac1{r^2}=s^2-2=1$, so the second factor is $1-1=0$.

**Answer: (C) $0$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-27.title: Compare altitudes
amc12-ahsme-1952-27.body:
Perimeters of equilateral triangles are proportional to their altitudes. The inscribed triangle's altitude is $\frac32R$ (the center lies $\frac23$ of the way down the altitude, at distance $R$ from the vertex). The first triangle's altitude is $R$. Ratio $R:\frac32R=2:3$.

**Answer: (E) $2:3$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-27.title: Side lengths
amc12-ahsme-1952-27.body:
Altitude $R$ gives side $\frac{2R}{\sqrt3}$, perimeter $2\sqrt3R$. The inscribed triangle has side $R\sqrt3$, perimeter $3\sqrt3R$. Ratio $2:3$.

**Answer: (E) $2:3$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-28.title: Test the choices
amc12-ahsme-1952-28.body:
$y=x^2+x+1$ gives $3,7,13,21,31$ ✓. (A) gives $3,7,11$ — fails at $x=3$. (B) gives $3,8$ — fails at $x=2$. (D) gives $0$ at $x=1$.

**Answer: (C) $y=x^2+x+1$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-28.title: Differences
amc12-ahsme-1952-28.body:
The differences $4,6,8,10$ increase by $2$, so $y$ is quadratic with leading coefficient $1$: $y-x^2=2,3,4,5,6=x+1$. So $y=x^2+x+1$.

**Answer: (C) $y=x^2+x+1$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-29.title: Similar right triangles
amc12-ahsme-1952-29.body:
Let $O$ be the center. $\angle CHD=90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle), so $DH=\sqrt{10^2-8^2}=6$. Triangles $COK$ and $CHD$ are similar (right angles at $O$ and $H$, common angle at $C$): $\frac{OK}{CO}=\frac{DH}{CH}=\frac68$, so $OK=\frac{15}{4}=3.75$. The segments of $AB$ are $5-3.75=1.25$ and $5+3.75=8.75$.

**Answer: (A) $1.25, 8.75$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-29.title: Power of a point
amc12-ahsme-1952-29.body:
$CK=\frac{CO}{\cos\angle OCK}=\frac{5}{8/10}=6.25$ (since $\cos\angle HCD=\frac{CH}{CD}=\frac8{10}$), so $KH=1.75$. By power of the point $K$: $AK\cdot KB=CK\cdot KH=10.9375$, with $AK+KB=10$. The numbers $1.25$ and $8.75$ satisfy both.

**Answer: (A) $1.25, 8.75$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-31.title: Choose pairs
amc12-ahsme-1952-31.body:
Each pair of points determines a line, and no line contains three of the points, so lines and pairs correspond: $\binom{12}{2}=66$.

**Answer: (D) $66$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-31.title: Count from each point
amc12-ahsme-1952-31.body:
Each point is joined to $11$ others: $12\cdot11=132$, but each line is counted from both ends: $66$.

**Answer: (D) $66$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-32.title: Time = distance/rate
amc12-ahsme-1952-32.body:
$K$ covers $30$ miles at $x$ mph, so his time is $\frac{30}{x}$ hours. (The other information is not needed for this question.)

**Answer: (D) $\frac{30}{x}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-32.title: Avoid the trap
amc12-ahsme-1952-32.body:
$M$'s rate is $x-\frac13$, so $M$'s time would be $\frac{30}{x-1/3}$; choice (C) uses $x+\frac13$, which is neither. $K$'s own time is simply $\frac{30}{x}$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{30}{x}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-33.title: Compute with perimeter $P$
amc12-ahsme-1952-33.body:
Square: side $\frac P4$, area $\frac{P^2}{16}$. Circle: radius $\frac{P}{2\pi}$, area $\frac{P^2}{4\pi}$. Since $4\pi<16$, the circle's area is greater.

**Answer: (B) the area of the circle is the greater**

amc12-ahsme-1952-33.title: Example
amc12-ahsme-1952-33.body:
Perimeter $4$: the square has area $1$; the circle has radius $\frac2\pi$ and area $\frac4\pi\approx1.27$. The ratio $\frac4\pi$ is not $\pi$.

**Answer: (B) the area of the circle is the greater**

amc12-ahsme-1952-34.title: Test $p=50$
amc12-ahsme-1952-34.body:
Up $50\%$ then down $50\%$ multiplies by $1.5\cdot0.5=0.75$, so the original price was $\frac43$ dollars. (E): $\frac{10000}{7500}=\frac43$ ✓. (D) gives $1-\frac{2500}{7500}=\frac23$.

**Answer: (E) $\frac{10000}{10000-p^2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-35.title: Rationalize in two steps
amc12-ahsme-1952-35.body:
Multiply by $\sqrt2+\sqrt3+\sqrt5$: the denominator becomes $(\sqrt2+\sqrt3)^2-5=2\sqrt6$ and the numerator $2+\sqrt6+\sqrt{10}$. Then multiply by $\frac{\sqrt6}{\sqrt6}$: $\frac{2\sqrt6+6+\sqrt{60}}{12}=\frac{6+2\sqrt6+2\sqrt{15}}{12}=\frac{3+\sqrt6+\sqrt{15}}{6}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac {3 + \sqrt {6} + \sqrt {15}}{6}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-36.title: Cancel the common factor
amc12-ahsme-1952-36.body:
$\frac{x^3+1}{x^2-1}=\frac{(x+1)(x^2-x+1)}{(x+1)(x-1)}=\frac{x^2-x+1}{x-1}$ for $x\ne-1$. At $x=-1$ this is $\frac{3}{-2}=-\frac32$, so that value makes the function continuous.

**Answer: (E) $-\frac{3}{2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-36.title: Derivatives (L'Hôpital)
amc12-ahsme-1952-36.body:
Both numerator and denominator vanish at $x=-1$. The limit equals the ratio of derivatives: $\frac{3x^2}{2x}\big|_{x=-1}=\frac{3}{-2}=-\frac32$.

**Answer: (E) $-\frac{3}{2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-37.title: Circle minus two segments
amc12-ahsme-1952-37.body:
Equal chords are equidistant from the center, so each is $4$ in from it. Each chord subtends a central angle of $120^\circ$ ($\cos\frac\theta2=\frac48$). One segment has area $\frac13\cdot64\pi-\frac12\cdot64\sin120^\circ=\frac{64\pi}3-16\sqrt3$. The region between is $64\pi-2\left(\frac{64\pi}3-16\sqrt3\right)=\frac{64\pi}{3}+32\sqrt3=32\sqrt3+21\frac13\pi$.

**Answer: (B) $32\sqrt{3}+21\frac{1}{3}\pi$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-37.title: Sectors plus triangles
amc12-ahsme-1952-37.body:
Join the center $O$ to the four chord endpoints. The region between the chords splits into two isosceles triangles with apex $O$ and base a chord (base $2\sqrt{64-16}=8\sqrt3$, height $4$, area $16\sqrt3$ each) and two sectors on the left and right. The chords take up $2\cdot120^\circ$ of central angle, so the two sectors total $120^\circ$, area $\frac13\cdot64\pi=\frac{64\pi}3$. Total $32\sqrt3+\frac{64\pi}{3}$.

**Answer: (B) $32\sqrt{3}+21\frac{1}{3}\pi$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-38.title: Sum of the bases
amc12-ahsme-1952-38.body:
$\frac{b_1+b_2}{2}\cdot50=1400$ gives $b_1+b_2=56$. With $b_1=8m$, $b_2=8n$: $m+n=7$ with positive integers. Unordered pairs: $\{1,6\},\{2,5\},\{3,4\}$, i.e. bases $(8,48),(16,40),(24,32)$. Three solutions.

**Answer: (D) three**

amc12-ahsme-1952-38.title: List
amc12-ahsme-1952-38.body:
Bases must be positive multiples of $8$ adding to $56$: $8+48$, $16+40$, $24+32$ (swapping the bases gives the same trapezoid shape data, and $28+28$ is not a multiple of $8$). So there are $3$.

**Answer: (D) three**

amc12-ahsme-1952-39.title: Example
amc12-ahsme-1952-39.body:
A $3\times4$ rectangle: $p=14$, $d=5$. (A) gives $\frac{\sqrt{200-196}}{2}=1$ ✓; (C) gives $\frac{\sqrt{150-196}}2$, not real.

**Answer: (A) $\frac {\sqrt {8d^2 - p^2}}{2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-40.title: Second differences
amc12-ahsme-1952-40.body:
For a quadratic at equally spaced points the second differences are constant. The first differences are $125,127,131,129,133,135,137$, and the second differences $2,4,-2,4,2,2$. The pattern $2,2,2,\dots$ is broken around the fourth value: replacing $4227$ by $4225$ gives first differences $125,127,129,131,133,135,137$. So the wrong value is $4227$, which is not among (A)–(D).

**Answer: (E) none of these**

amc12-ahsme-1952-40.title: Recognize squares
amc12-ahsme-1952-40.body:
The values are $62^2,63^2,64^2,\,?\,,66^2,67^2,68^2,69^2$, and $65^2=4225\ne4227$. All listed choices are correct squares; the incorrect entry $4227$ is not offered.

**Answer: (E) none of these**

amc12-ahsme-1952-42.title: Subtract
amc12-ahsme-1952-42.body:
From (C) and (B): $10^{r+s}D-10^rD=PQ.QQQ\ldots-P.QQQ\ldots$. The repeating tails cancel, giving $10^r(10^s-1)D=PQ-P$, where $PQ$ is the integer with digits of $P$ followed by $Q$. This is not $Q(P-1)$, so (D) is incorrect. (A), (B), (C), (E) just shift the decimal point.

**Answer: (D)**

amc12-ahsme-1952-43.title: It is constant
amc12-ahsme-1952-43.body:
Each small semicircle has diameter $\frac dn$ and arc length $\frac{\pi d}{2n}$. The $n$ arcs together have length $\frac{\pi d}{2}$ — exactly the original semicircumference, for every $n$. So the limit is the semicircumference (even though the curve gets closer and closer to the diameter).

**Answer: (A) equal to the semi-circumference of the original circle**

amc12-ahsme-1952-43.title: Scaling
amc12-ahsme-1952-43.body:
Arc length scales linearly: halving the diameter halves the semicircle. Two semicircles on the halves have total length equal to one on the whole, and repeating the argument shows the total never changes from $\frac{\pi d}{2}$.

**Answer: (A) equal to the semi-circumference of the original circle**

amc12-ahsme-1952-44.title: Add the two numbers
amc12-ahsme-1952-44.body:
Let the number be $10a+b=k(a+b)$. The reversed number is $10b+a$. Adding: $(10a+b)+(10b+a)=11(a+b)$, so $10b+a=11(a+b)-k(a+b)=(11-k)(a+b)$.

**Answer: (C) $11-k$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-45.title: AM–GM–HM
amc12-ahsme-1952-45.body:
AM $>$ GM: $\frac{a+b}2>\sqrt{ab}$ because $\frac{a+b}{2}-\sqrt{ab}=\frac{(\sqrt a-\sqrt b)^2}{2}>0$. GM $>$ HM: since $a+b>2\sqrt{ab}$, we get $\frac{2ab}{a+b}<\frac{2ab}{2\sqrt{ab}}=\sqrt{ab}$. So $\frac{a+b}{2}>\sqrt{ab}>\frac{2ab}{a+b}$.

**Answer: (E)**

amc12-ahsme-1952-46.title: Difference of squares
amc12-ahsme-1952-46.body:
With sides $l>w$ and diagonal $d$: the new area is $(d+l)(d-l)=d^2-l^2=w^2$, the area of a square on the smaller side.

**Answer: (C)**

amc12-ahsme-1952-46.title: Example
amc12-ahsme-1952-46.body:
A $3\times4$ rectangle has diagonal $5$. New rectangle: $9\times1$, area $9=3^2$. The given rectangle has area $12$, so (A), (B) fail; (D) gives $16$, (E) gives $15$.

**Answer: (C)**

amc12-ahsme-1952-48.title: Relative speeds
amc12-ahsme-1952-48.body:
With speeds $u>v$: same direction, the gap closes at $u-v$, so $u-v=\frac kr$; opposite directions, $u+v=\frac kt$. Then $u=\frac k2\left(\frac1t+\frac1r\right)$, $v=\frac k2\left(\frac1t-\frac1r\right)$, and $\frac uv=\frac{r+t}{r-t}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac {r + t}{r - t}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-48.title: Numbers
amc12-ahsme-1952-48.body:
Speeds $3$ and $1$, $k=12$: same direction they meet after $\frac{12}{2}=6$ h ($r=6$), opposite after $\frac{12}{4}=3$ h ($t=3$). (A): $\frac{9}{3}=3$ ✓.

**Answer: (A) $\frac {r + t}{r - t}$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-49.title: Three big triangles
amc12-ahsme-1952-49.body:
Let $[ABC]=1$. Since $CD=\frac13CB$, $[ADC]=\frac13$. Since $AN_1=\frac67AD$, $[AN_1C]=\frac67\cdot\frac13=\frac27$. In the same way $[BN_2A]=\frac27$ and $[CN_3B]=\frac27$. These three triangles do not overlap, and together with triangle $N_1N_2N_3$ they cover $ABC$ exactly (each is one small corner triangle plus one quadrilateral of the figure). So $[N_1N_2N_3]=1-3\cdot\frac27=\frac17$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{1}{7}\triangle ABC$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-49.title: Coordinates
amc12-ahsme-1952-49.body:
Place $B=(0,0)$, $C=(3,0)$, $A=(0,3)$, so $[ABC]=\frac92$, $D=(2,0)$, $E=(1,2)$, $F=(0,1)$. Line $AD$ is $(2s,3-3s)$ and line $BE$ is $y=2x$; they meet at $s=\frac37$: $N_2=\left(\frac67,\frac{12}7\right)$. Similarly $N_1=\left(\frac{12}7,\frac37\right)$ (at $s=\frac67$) and $N_3=\left(\frac37,\frac67\right)$. By the shoelace formula, $[N_1N_2N_3]=\frac12\left|\left(-\frac67\right)\cdot\frac37-\frac97\cdot\left(-\frac97\right)\right|=\frac12\cdot\frac{63}{49}=\frac{9}{14}$, and $\frac{9/14}{9/2}=\frac17$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{1}{7}\triangle ABC$**

amc12-ahsme-1952-50.title: Group in pairs
amc12-ahsme-1952-50.body:
After the first term, group $\left(\frac14\sqrt2+\frac14\right)+\left(\frac1{16}\sqrt2+\frac1{16}\right)+\dots=(1+\sqrt2)\cdot\frac13$. Adding $1$: $\frac{3+1+\sqrt2}{3}=\frac{4+\sqrt2}{3}$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{1}{3}(4+\sqrt{2})$**
